summary: Corrects and clarifies how the Label Distribution Protocol behaves when run over IPv6, alone or alongside IPv4. It updates RFCs 5036 and 6720 and fixes ambiguities that could hurt interoperability.

eli5.summary: A rulebook for a delivery system had gaps in how it worked on the newer address system. This patch fills in the gaps.

subtitle: The rules LDP was missing for running label distribution over IPv6, alone or side by side with IPv4.

tldr.problem: The Label Distribution Protocol specification in RFC 5036 was vague about IPv6: which multicast address to use for discovery, what to do when a router speaks both IPv4 and IPv6, and how to find the right peer when link-local addresses repeat.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7552 fixes these gaps with explicit rules: a common LDP Identifier for both address families, link-local multicast discovery with a Hop Limit of 255, one session per pair of routers, and a new Dual-Stack capability TLV that settles which transport (IPv4 or IPv6) the session uses.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 5036 and RFC 6720 so that IPv6-only and dual-stack LDP networks behave predictably, and it adds safeguards so upgraded routers do not break older IPv4-only peers.

facts.label: IPv6 Hop Limit on Link Hellos

today: RFC 7552 is a Standards Track document (Proposed Standard) that updates RFC 5036 and RFC 6720, and no later RFC is recorded as updating or obsoleting it.

sections.title: Why LDP Needed IPv6 Fixes
sections.content:
The Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) in RFC 5036 lets Label Switching Routers (LSRs) exchange bindings between a Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) and a label. It is described as working over IPv4, IPv6, or both, which the RFC calls dual-stack. In practice the text lacked detail for IPv6.

RFC 7552 lists eight deficiencies: no rule for mapping a packet to an LSP whose FEC holds an IPv6 address; no IPv6 details for the LDP Identifier; no choice of IPv6 destination or source address for discovery; no rule for IPv4 and IPv6 Transport Address objects in a Hello, and the two transport connections that could follow; no rule for advertising IPv4 and IPv6 addresses; none for advertising IPv4 and IPv6 label bindings; none for duplicate link-local next-hop addresses; and no built-in Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM) for LDP over IPv6, a gap in RFC 6720.

The document closes the IPv6 MPLS gap identified in RFC 7439. It covers three topologies: routers joined by one dual-stack interface, by two single-stack interfaces (one IPv4, one IPv6), or by a single-stack interface on each side, plus extended (targeted) discovery in either family.
sections.eli5: The old rulebook said the system could work with the new kind of address but never said how. This document writes down the missing steps.

sections.title: LSP Mapping and LDP Identifiers
sections.content:
RFC 5036 said a packet bound for a particular egress router maps to an LSP whose Address Prefix FEC element is a /32 address of that router. That is right for IPv4 but not for IPv6, where a router may have a /64, /96, /128 or other prefix length. RFC 7552 rewrites the rule to say the FEC element is simply an IPv4 or IPv6 address of that router.

For identity, the LSR Id stays a 32-bit unsigned non-zero integer even on an IPv6 router, and one common LDP Identifier (the same LSR Id and label space id) is used for both address families. The old rule that an LSR MUST advertise the same transport address in all Hellos for a label space is now applied per address family, which lets the per-platform label space be shared between IPv4 and IPv6.

An appendix explains why the LSR Id is still 32 bits: it identifies the router globally within the MPLS network, but need not map to any IPv4 address, be routable or resolve in DNS. In IPv6-only networks it must be derived some other way that guarantees uniqueness, as with the BGP Identifier and the OSPF router Id. The value 0.0.0.0 is reserved and may not be used with IPv6.
sections.eli5: Every delivery truck keeps one ID number, no matter which kind of road it drives on. The old rule about exact address sizes is loosened so it works for the longer new addresses.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery over IPv6
sections.content:
LSRs find each other with Hello messages. If dual-stack LDP is enabled on an interface or for a targeted neighbor, the LSR MUST send both IPv6 and IPv4 Hellos carrying the same LDP Identifier. If only one family is enabled, it sends only that family's Hellos.

For basic (link) discovery, IPv6 offers three all-routers multicast groups: ff01:0:0:0:0:0:0:2 (interface-local), ff02:0:0:0:0:0:0:2 (link-local) and ff05:0:0:0:0:0:0:2 (site-local). RFC 7552 picks the link-local one as the destination for IPv6 Link Hellos and says a Hello arriving on any other destination MUST be dropped. The source address MUST be the sender's link-local IPv6 address, and the Hop Limit MUST be 255, checked on receipt before any LDP processing, as in RFC 5082.

For extended discovery, where targeted Hellos go to a unicast address, the one IPv6 rule is that link-local addresses MUST NOT be used as the source or destination. On a dual-stack interface an LSR SHOULD keep Hello adjacencies for both families, though it may keep receive-side adjacencies only for the family that carried the session.
sections.eli5: Routers shout hello on a shared neighborhood channel. The rules say which channel to use and that the shout must come from right next door, so far-away strangers cannot fake it.

sections.title: Setting Up and Keeping a Session
sections.content:
After discovery, two LSRs open a TCP transport connection and then initialize an LDP session. RFC 7552 sets these rules for the Transport Address object: a Hello MUST NOT carry both an IPv4 and an IPv6 one, and it carries only the family of the packet it rides in; a dual-stack LSR MUST send separate Hellos for each family; a receiver SHOULD accept the first object of a given family and ignore the rest. Targeted Hellos MUST use a global unicast IPv6 address, and for Link Hellos a global unicast address is preferred over unique-local or link-local.

Two routers maintain only one session, however many Hello adjacencies they have. A dual-stack LSR MUST NOT start or accept a new TCP connection if it already has an LDPoIPv4 or LDPoIPv6 session for the same LDP Identifier with that peer. A dual-stack LSR SHOULD prefer LDP over IPv6, and ideally sends IPv6 Link Hellos before IPv4 ones when an interface comes into service.

If the last Hello adjacency of the family used by the session goes down, the session MUST be reset. Otherwise it stays up. If a session is torn down for any reason, the LSRs SHOULD try to establish a new one by the same procedure.
sections.eli5: Two neighbors can talk by phone or by letter, but only one conversation is allowed at a time. They agree on which one first, and if that line goes dead, they start over.

sections.title: The Dual-Stack Capability TLV
sections.content:
RFC 5036 decides which side opens the TCP connection (active) and which waits (passive) by comparing transport addresses. With two address families a router could be active in one and passive in the other, and the session would never form. To avoid this, a dual-stack LSR MUST put a new Dual-Stack capability TLV (code point 0x0701) in every Hello. Its 4-bit TR field announces the preference: 0100 for LDP over IPv4, or 0110 for LDP over IPv6, which is the default.

On receipt, a dual-stack LSR checks the TLV. If the peer's preference differs from its own or is not recognized, it MUST discard the Hello and log an error, and if a session exists it MUST send a fatal Notification with status code Transport Connection Mismatch (0x00000032) and reset it. If the preferences match, the roles are worked out using the IPv4 or IPv6 transport address as RFC 5036 describes.

If the TLV is missing, Hellos of one family only mean a legacy single-stack neighbor, and a session of that family SHOULD be set up. But Hellos of both families without the TLV mark a noncompliant dual-stack neighbor, which gets no session; the status code is Dual-Stack Noncompliance (0x00000033). The same TR value MUST appear in all Hellos for the same label space to the same peer. A single-stack LSR SHOULD ignore the TLV. The document notes that a flag in the Hello message was rejected as an alternative because it would linger even after dual-stack networks are gone.
sections.eli5: Two friends who can talk by phone or text each say which they prefer. If they pick different ways, they sort it out right away, so nobody ends up waiting for the other to call.

sections.title: Distributing Addresses and Labels
sections.content:
Some older IPv4-only LSRs do not handle IPv6 content gracefully. They may reset the session on seeing IPv6 address bindings or IPv6 FEC label bindings, or abort an entire Label Mapping message that mixes IPv4 and IPv6 FECs and so discard the IPv4 labels too. The appendices say this would make IPv6 LDP undeployable in existing networks. So an LSR MUST NOT send IPv6 bindings to a peer determined to be a legacy LSR, and the Dual-Stack capability TLV is how that is determined.

An LSR MUST NOT advertise IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses in Address messages, and MUST ignore them if received. It MUST NOT allocate or advertise label bindings for link-local or IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses either. The reason given is the consensus of the 6MAN and V6OPS working groups against such addresses in routing tables and LDP databases.

For a dual-stack peer, the rules are the same for addresses and labels. No TLV in IPv4 Hellos means no IPv6 content. The TLV in IPv4 or IPv6 Hellos means both families are advertised. No TLV in IPv6 Hellos means IPv6 only. An LSR MAY narrow this further by negotiating IP capability per family as in RFC 7473. When switching a peer from single-stack to dual-stack, an LSR SHOULD use the Typed Wildcard FEC procedures of RFC 5918 to relearn bindings without resetting the session.
sections.eli5: Before sending a neighbor a parcel with the new kind of label, the router checks whether the neighbor can read it. If not, it sends only the old kind, so nothing gets thrown away.

sections.title: Duplicate Link-Local Next Hops
sections.content:
To find the label for a FEC, an LSR takes the IP routing next-hop address and looks it up in its peer address database, which Address messages fill in, to find the LDP peer. That fails with IPv6 link-local addresses. Interior IPv6 routing protocols can use link-local addresses as next hops, and RFC 4291 lets one link-local address be used on more than one link, so two peers can have the same next-hop address.

The fix is to use the next-hop interface as well as the address. Address-based lookup uses the peer address database built from Address messages, and interface-based lookup uses the Hello adjacency and interface database built from Hello messages. Together they uniquely identify the peer. As a scaling optimization, an LSR may advertise only link-local IPv6 addresses in its Address message if the peer uses only link-local addresses as next hops.
sections.eli5: If two houses on different streets share a street number, you also need the street name to find the right one. Routers use the cable they are plugged into as the street name.

sections.title: TTL Security and Other Security Notes
sections.content:
RFC 7552 requires the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM) for IPv6 LDP Link Hello packets: Hop Limit set to 255 and checked on receipt, per Section 3 of RFC 5082. It further recommends enabling GTSM for the LDP TCP connection over IPv6. The goal is to protect IPv6 LDP sessions from off-link attacks. RFC 6720 allows GTSM to be turned off per peer, statically or dynamically. Because GTSM applies only to single-hop sessions, any LDP feature relying on a multi-hop session needs GTSM disabled.

The Security Considerations section says the document only clarifies existing LDP behavior and defines no new protocol procedures, so it adds no new security issues. The issues of RFC 5036 still apply. The document points out that it reduces the chance of off-link attacks over IPv6 through GTSM, and that it allows IPsec to be used for IPv6 protection.
sections.eli5: Each message carries a counter that goes down at every hop. If a message claims to be from next door but its counter shows it traveled far, it is thrown away.

fields.name: U
fields.desc: U bit, set to 1 as RFC 5036 specifies.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: F bit, set to 0 as RFC 5036 specifies.

fields.name: TR
fields.desc: Transport Connection Preference: 0100 for LDPoIPv4, 0110 for LDPoIPv6 (default).

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.
